title: FHA financing opens to build-to-rent: What developers need to know
summary: HUD expands FHA financing eligibility to build-to-rent communities. Learn which projects qualify and what developers need to know before applying.
body_markdown:
HUD has expanded[FHA](https://www.walkerdunlop.com/services/capital-markets/fha) multifamily mortgage insurance eligibility to qualifying build-to-rent (BTR) communities. Effective immediately, Mortgagee Letter 2026-12 allows rental developments consisting of detached single-family homes, duplexes, and triplexes to be considered under the same terms and conditions as traditional[multifamily](https://www.walkerdunlop.com/specialties-sectors/conventional-multifamily) properties, subject to BTR-specific requirements.


The guidance gives developers and owners a clearer basis for evaluating FHA-insured financing. Project age, site configuration, ownership restrictions, and operating assumptions will determine which communities qualify and how applications are underwritten.


## Which projects qualify?


The letter establishes eligibility under two programs:


- **Section 221(d)(4):** New construction only.
- **Section 223(f):** Acquisition or refinancing of recently developed rental housing with a certificate of occupancy dated less than three years before application.


Older BTR communities outside that three-year window are not eligible under this expansion.


Each development must contain at least five dwelling units on a cohesive, contiguous site, developed for long-term rental use and operated as one multifamily property. A single tax parcel is preferred, although multiple contiguous parcels comprising the insured site are acceptable. Interspersed privately owned homes or parcels are not allowed.


Developers should also weigh the restrictions against their exit plans. HUD will not approve sales of individual parcels or buildings, or any partial release of collateral, during the insured loan term.


Projects combining BTR homes with traditional multifamily buildings may qualify, provided the application addresses the underwriting and accessibility requirements associated with the mix. Manufactured and modular construction are generally acceptable, but any challenges involving construction advances must be reviewed.


## Underwriting must account for BTR operations


HUD expects sponsors, contractors, and management agents to demonstrate successful experience developing and operating similar projects in type and scale. Applications must also support assumptions about how the community will lease and operate.


**Lease-up and operating deficit escrow:** For new construction, HUD will consider an absorption period of up to 24 months, recognizing that homes may be delivered and leased while construction continues. Applications must include a detailed construction schedule and leasing strategy supported by recent comparable BTR lease-up activity.


Initial operating deficit escrow must equal at least the greater of 3 percent of the loan amount or four months of debt service. That minimum does not replace the lender’s analysis of the funds the project will need.


**Vacancy:** Market-rate projects must use the greater of 7 percent or the market-supported vacancy rate from comparable properties. Affordable projects may justify an assumption below 7 percent based on market conditions, area median income targets, the duration of affordability restrictions, and the rent advantage, subject to a 5 percent minimum. Smaller communities may require higher assumptions because each vacant home has a greater effect on income.


**Expenses and reserves:** Low-density layouts can increase grounds, road, and exterior maintenance costs. HUD discourages relying solely on traditional apartment expense data; budgets should draw on comparable stabilized BTR properties, sponsor or management budgets, and industry benchmarks.


Developers should also anticipate higher initial and annual replacement reserve deposits. A community with more individual buildings has more roofs, exterior walls, windows, and other components to maintain and replace.


## Management and governance matter


Properties must be professionally managed, with staffing, amenities, and services consistent with comparable communities. An on-site management office and maintenance staff are not universally required. Off-site operations must have a local presence and enough staff to serve the property and the rest of the portfolio.


Amenities should reflect the market. Private yards and garages may be more prevalent than clubhouses or pools, and the lender must account for those differences when evaluating comparable properties.


An HOA or other master-planned community governing structure cannot interfere with the owner’s full management control or HUD’s enforcement of program requirements. Lenders must disclose these arrangements and complete their analysis and resolve conflicts before application.


## Accessibility depends on the buildings and their use


Detached homes, duplexes, and triplexes do not meet the definition of covered multifamily dwellings and are exempt from specified Fair Housing Act accessibility design requirements within those buildings and units. HUD nevertheless strongly encourages those features.


Common-use areas and site amenities still require accessible routes, entries, and other applicable features. In mixed developments, covered multifamily buildings containing four or more units remain subject to the applicable design requirements.


Other accessibility obligations may apply, including Section 504 when federal assistance is involved and the Americans with Disabilities Act for public accommodations. Where federal, state, or local requirements differ, the more stringent requirements apply.


## Start with a project-level review


For developers planning new BTR communities or owners evaluating a recent completion, the first step is to review the project’s site boundaries, certificate-of-occupancy timing, ownership structure, and operating budget with an FHA lender.


The new guidance makes those early discussions more concrete. Developers can assess eligibility, identify design or governance issues, and establish the market evidence needed to support an application.
